name: Lister Housing Co-operative (Georgian Tenements)
description: This block of Georgian tenements, built between 1816 and 1824 around Heriot Place, Keir Street and Lauriston Place, had fallen into serious disrepair by the 1970s. Rather than see it demolished, residents formed one of Edinburgh's early tenant-led housing co-operatives, taking ownership of the buildings and securing government funding for a full rehabilitation carried out between 1978 and 1982 - work that went on to win a Saltire Award. Part of the funding came through the Lister Trust, set up in memory of Joseph Lister, the pioneer of antiseptic surgery, whose old Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh stands directly across Lauriston Place.
interesting_fact: In the mid-1980s the co-operative expanded again, taking on a U-shaped tenement across the road that the Royal Infirmary itself had earmarked for demolition. The 1990-92 rescue created 50 new flats at a cost of £5.5 million, making it the highest-value housing project in Scotland at the time. The co-operative has since paid off every loan it took out and now owns all of its properties outright, a rare outcome for a scheme of this size and age.
source_notes: All details from the Lister Housing Co-operative's own published history page. Distinct from the Old Royal Infirmary POI already drafted for leg 13 - that entry covers the Bryce hospital buildings and their Quartermile conversion, this one covers a separate residential block and its community-led rescue, connected only by the shared Joseph Lister naming and the Infirmary's demolition plans for the 1990s annexe. name: Graham Street Synagogue (site)
address: Keir Street (formerly Graham Street), Edinburgh EH3 9EU
description: Keir Street was known as Graham Street until 1966, and from 1898 it was home to Edinburgh's synagogue - a former Greyfriars Free Church building converted for Jewish worship at a cost of around £4,000, roughly £300,000 today. It served a large part of the city's Jewish community, many of them living across the south side in areas like Morningside, complete with its own Sunday school and a handful of community-run shops nearby. Rabbi Salis Daiches, a prominent figure in Edinburgh Jewish life, led the congregation here in the early twentieth century.
interesting_fact: The congregation eventually outgrew the building and moved to a purpose-built synagogue on Salisbury Road, consecrated in 1932 and still in use today. The old Graham Street building was later demolished, and the street itself was renamed Keir Street in 1966, erasing both names that once marked this corner of the city's Jewish history from the map entirely. It was Edinburgh's third synagogue site in total, following earlier premises in a rented tenement room at Richmond Court from 1817 and then in Park Place from 1868 - a slow migration south and west across the Old Town as the congregation grew.

No exact building number survives in available sources, so an estimated coordinate on Keir Street is used - Google Places has no listing for the vanished building itself.
